title: Μέγαρον καθαιρόμενον
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: At Telemachus's call the nurse Eurycleia opens the doors and goes with him to the hall, where she finds Odysseus spattered with blood among the dead, like a lion that has fed on an ox. She is about to cry out in triumph, but Odysseus checks her: it is not right to exult over slain men, whom the gods and their own cruel deeds have brought down. At his bidding she tells him of the fifty maidservants, of whom twelve have shamed the house, and Odysseus sets the hall's cleaning in motion: the dead are carried out, the chairs and tables washed, the floor scraped. The twelve are penned in the yard between the round house and the fence, and Telemachus, refusing them a clean death, hangs them from a ship's cable like thrushes or doves caught in a net. Melanthius is led out and mutilated. Odysseus then has sulphur and fire brought and fumigates the hall, the house and the courtyard, and the women who remain come out with torches to greet him; a longing to weep rises in him, and he knows them all.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἐφώνησεν, τῇ δ’ ἄπτερος ἔπλετο μῦθος,
ὤϊξεν δὲ θύρας μεγάρων εὖ ναιεταόντων,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephōnēsen, tēi d’ apteros epleto mythos,
ōïxen de thyras megarōn eu naietaontōn,
bē d’ imen·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and for her the speech was wingless; she opened the doors of the well-inhabited halls and set out,
sentences.n: Telemachus has just spoken to the nurse Eurycleia (395–397), and these words say what that speech did and what she did next. The first line is a line already published, and keeps its English: ἄπτερος 'wingless' is the opposite of the winged words (ἔπεα πτερόεντα) that introduce a reply; it may mean that she made no answer, which the Greek does not say. ἐφώνησεν and ὤϊξεν have no named subject: the first is Telemachus, and the second is taken to be the nurse, because τῇ 'for her' has just named her and Τηλέμαχος in the next unit is set against her. ἔπλετο is an unaugmented aorist of πέλομαι 'come to be, be'. ὤϊξεν is an aorist of the verb 'open' (Attic ἀνέῳξεν). μεγάρων εὖ ναιεταόντων 'of the well-inhabited halls' is a formula. βῆ is unaugmented (Attic ἔβη) and ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι 'go' (Attic ἰέναι): 'she set off to go'. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος πρόσθ’ ἡγεμόνευεν.
sentences.tr: autar Tēlemachos prosth’ hēgemoneuen.
sentences.l: but Telemachus in front was leading the way.
sentences.i: while Telemachus went ahead, leading the way.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ here is 'but, while', setting the two movements side by side: she goes, and Telemachus goes first. πρόσθ’ is πρόσθε 'in front, ahead' with its vowel elided, and ἡγεμόνευεν is the imperfect of ἡγεμονεύω 'lead the way', from ἡγεμών 'leader'. The sentence begins in the middle of the line, after the ano teleia at ἴμεν.

sentences.t:
εὗρεν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν,
αἵματι καὶ λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένον ὥστε λέοντα,
ὅς ῥά τε βεβρωκὼς βοὸς ἔρχεται ἀγραύλοιο·
sentences.tr:
heuren epeit’ Odysēa meta ktamenoisi nekyssin,
haimati kai lythrōi pepalagmenon hōste leonta,
hos rha te bebrōkōs boos erchetai agrauloio·
sentences.i: She found Odysseus then among the slain corpses, spattered with blood and gore, like a lion that has eaten of a field-dwelling ox and goes on its way;
sentences.n: εὗρεν has no stated subject; it is the nurse, who has just set out. κταμένοισι is the dative plural of κτάμενος, an old aorist participle of κτείνω 'kill' with passive sense, 'slain', and νέκυσσιν is the dative plural of νέκυς 'corpse' with doubled σ. πεπαλαγμένον is the perfect passive participle of παλάσσω 'spatter', agreeing with Ὀδυσῆα; λύθρος is the filth and gore of a battlefield or slaughter. The comparison is the beginning of a simile: ὥστε λέοντα 'like a lion', then ὅς ῥά τε, with epic τε marking what is true of lions in general. βεβρωκώς is the perfect participle of βιβρώσκω 'eat', here with the genitive βοός, 'having eaten of an ox'. ἀγραύλοιο, from ἀγρός 'field' and αὐλή 'fold', means living out in the fields, and is an epithet of oxen.

sentences.t:
πᾶν δ’ ἄρα οἱ στῆθός τε παρήϊά τ’ ἀμφοτέρωθεν
αἱματόεντα πέλει, δεινὸς δ’ εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
pan d’ ara hoi stēthos te parēïa t’ amphoterōthen
haimatoenta pelei, deinos d’ eis ōpa idesthai·
sentences.l:
and all his chest and his cheeks on both sides,
is bloody, and he is dreadful to look at in the face;
sentences.i: his whole chest and both his cheeks are bloody, and he is dreadful to look upon;
sentences.n: The simile goes on, and its verbs are in the present, because it describes what any such lion is like. οἱ is the dative of the person concerned, 'his' (the lion's); πᾶν agrees with στῆθος, 'all the chest', and the cheeks are added after it. παρήϊά is the cheeks (the neuter plural of παρήϊον, with the epic diaeresis). αἱματόεντα is αἷμα 'blood' with -όεις 'full of', so 'bloody'. πέλει is a present of πέλομαι, here simply 'is'. δεινός is 'dreadful', and εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι is 'to see to the face', an infinitive of respect, 'to look upon'.

sentences.t: ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς πεπάλακτο πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν.
sentences.tr: hōs Odyseus pepalakto podas kai cheiras hyperthen.
sentences.l: so Odysseus was spattered, feet and hands, above.
sentences.i: That was how Odysseus was spattered, over his feet and hands.
sentences.n: The simile is closed with ὥς 'so' and applied to Odysseus. πεπάλακτο is the pluperfect passive of παλάσσω, the same verb as πεπαλαγμένον in line 402, and πόδας καὶ χεῖρας is an accusative of respect, 'as to his feet and hands'. ὕπερθεν is 'above, on top': what it adds here is not made clear by the Greek, and the English leaves it as it stands.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὡς οὖν νέκυάς τε καὶ ἄσπετον εἴσιδεν αἷμα,
ἴθυσέν ῥ’ ὀλολύξαι, ἐπεὶ μέγα εἴσιδεν ἔργον·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ hōs oun nekyas te kai aspeton eisiden haima,
ithysen rh’ ololyxai, epei mega eisiden ergon·
sentences.l:
And she, when then she saw the corpses and the boundless blood,
made straight to raise the cry, since she saw a great deed;
sentences.i: And when she saw the corpses and the boundless blood, she rushed to raise a cry, because she saw a great deed;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is the nurse. ὡς here is 'when'; εἴσιδεν is an unaugmented aorist of εἰσοράω 'look at, see', repeated in the next line. νέκυάς has a short -υας ending, the accusative plural of νέκυς. ἄσπετον is 'boundless, not to be told'. ἴθυσεν is an aorist of ἰθύω 'go straight at, press on', followed by the infinitive ὀλολύξαι. ὀλολύζω is a loud cry made by women, of prayer to a god or of triumph; Odysseus's answer in the next lines shows that she meant exultation. ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle of lively narrative.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ Ὀδυσεὺς κατέρυκε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱεμένην περ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
all’ Odyseus kateryke kai eschethen hiemenēn per,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
But Odysseus held her back and restrained her, eager though she was,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: But Odysseus held her back and checked her, eager as she was, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: The first line has the same verbs as a line already published, with the feminine ἱεμένην in place of the masculine and plural forms there. κατέρυκε is an unaugmented imperfect of κατερύκω 'hold back' and ἔσχεθεν a by-form of the aorist ἔσχον of ἔχω, 'restrained'. ἱεμένην is the middle participle of ἵημι 'press forward, be eager', and περ makes it concessive: 'eager though she was'. The second line is a whole line already published, and keeps its English: φωνήσας is literally 'having made a sound', that is 'lifting his voice', and ἔπεα πτερόεντα is the formula 'winged words', with προσηύδα an unaugmented imperfect of προσαυδάω 'speak to'.

sentences.t: ἐν θυμῷ, γρηῦ, χαῖρε καὶ ἴσχεο μηδ’ ὀλόλυζε·
sentences.tr: en thymōi, grēu, chaire kai ischeo mēd’ ololyze·
sentences.l: “In your heart, old woman, rejoice, and hold yourself back, and do not raise the cry;
sentences.i: “Rejoice in your heart, old woman, but hold yourself back and do not cry out;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks. γρηῦ is the vocative of γρηῦς 'old woman'. χαῖρε is the imperative of χαίρω 'rejoice', not a greeting here; ἐν θυμῷ 'in your heart' means that the joy is to stay inside. ἴσχεο is the imperative of ἴσχομαι 'hold yourself back', and the ending -εο is the uncontracted -ου. μηδ’ ὀλόλυζε repeats the verb of the cry that the nurse was about to raise.

sentences.t: οὐχ ὁσίη κταμένοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι.
sentences.tr: ouch hosiē ktamenoisin ep’ andrasin euchetaasthai.
sentences.l: not holy is it, over slain men, to vaunt.
sentences.i: It is not right to exult over slain men.
sentences.n: οὐχ ὁσίη has no verb, and 'is' is understood. ὁσίη is what divine custom allows, as opposed to what human law allows: 'holy' in the literal English, 'right' in the plain English. κταμένοισιν is the dative plural 'slain' again. εὐχετάασθαι is an uncontracted infinitive of εὐχετάομαι (Attic εὐχετᾶσθαι), which means both 'pray' and 'make a boast'; with ἐπί and the dative of the dead men it must be 'boast over, exult over'.

sentences.t: τούσδε δὲ μοῖρ’ ἐδάμασσε θεῶν καὶ σχέτλια ἔργα·
sentences.tr: tousde de moir’ edamasse theōn kai schetlia erga·
sentences.l: These men the portion of the gods subdued, and their cruel deeds;
sentences.i: These men were overcome by what the gods had portioned out, and by their cruel deeds;
sentences.n: τούσδε is 'these men', pointing at the corpses. μοῖρα is a share or allotted portion; μοῖρα θεῶν is the portion that the gods have measured out, and the English keeps the word 'portion' rather than 'fate'. The verb ἐδάμασσε is singular though it has two subjects, μοῖρα and σχέτλια ἔργα, because it agrees with the first of them, the one next to it. δαμάζω is 'subdue, overpower', and ἐδάμασσε is its aorist, with the doubled σ of the epic spelling. σχέτλια ἔργα is 'cruel deeds', with σχέτλιος 'cruel'.

sentences.t:
οὔ τινα γὰρ τίεσκον ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων,
οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν, ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκοιτο·
sentences.tr:
ou tina gar tieskon epichthoniōn anthrōpōn,
ou kakon oude men esthlon, hotis spheas eisaphikoito·
sentences.l:
for no one did they honour of men upon the earth,
neither bad nor yet good, whoever came to them;
sentences.i: for they honoured none of the men who live on the earth, neither bad nor good, whoever came to them;
sentences.n: The whole unit is a pair of lines already published, and keeps its English. τίεσκον is an imperfect with the iterative suffix -σκ-, which makes the action habitual: 'they used to honour' no one. ἐπιχθονίων is 'upon the earth', so 'men upon the earth'. ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκοιτο is a general clause: 'whoever came to them', with the optative of an action repeated again and again and σφέας the pronoun 'them'. In this passage the line states the suitors' offence: they paid no respect to a guest, whatever sort of man he was.

sentences.t: τῷ καὶ ἀτασθαλίῃσιν ἀεικέα πότμον ἐπέσπον.
sentences.tr: tōi kai atasthaliēisin aeikea potmon epespon.
sentences.l: Therefore too, by their wanton-follies, an unseemly doom they met.
sentences.i: That is why, through their wanton folly, they met an unseemly doom.
sentences.n: This is a line already published, and keeps its English. τῷ is 'therefore', with καί. ἀτασθαλίῃσιν is the dative plural of ἀτασθαλία in -ῃσιν, 'wanton folly', as in the proem. ἀεικέα πότμον is the formula 'unseemly doom', and ἐπέσπον is an unaugmented aorist of ἐφέπω, 'met, came upon'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι σὺ γυναῖκας ἐνὶ μεγάροις κατάλεξον,
αἵ τέ μ’ ἀτιμάζουσι καὶ αἳ νηλείτιδές εἰσιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi sy gynaikas eni megarois katalexon,
hai te m’ atimazousi kai hai nēleitides eisin.
sentences.l:
But come, to me do you the women in the halls list,
who both dishonour me and who are guiltless.”
sentences.i: But come, you tell me which women in the halls dishonour me and which are guiltless.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come'. κατάλεξον is the imperative of καταλέγω 'list, count off'; the pronoun σύ is there to put weight on the nurse, who is the one who knows. αἵ τε ... καὶ αἳ is 'those who ... and those who', the two classes of women. ἀτιμάζουσι is 'dishonour'. νηλείτιδες is from νηλειτής, 'free of guilt', and the English says 'guiltless'; the sense is known from context rather than from firm etymology, and here it is the opposite of 'dishonouring'. This ends Odysseus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is a whole line already published, and keeps its English. It is the reply-formula that has Eurycleia's standing description, φίλη τροφός 'the dear nurse', and αὖτε 'in turn'. τόν is the pronoun 'him', and προσέειπε the unaugmented aorist of προσεῖπον 'address'.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, τέκνον, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, teknon, alētheiēn katalexō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I to you, child, the truth will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, my child, I will tell you the truth.
sentences.n: Eurycleia answers. This is a whole line already published, and keeps its English. τοιγάρ is 'well then, therefore', and τοι is the enclitic 'to you'. τέκνον is 'child', used by the old woman who nursed him. ἀληθείην is the Ionic form of ἀλήθεια (Attic ἀλήθειαν), and καταλέξω the future of καταλέγω 'recount'.

sentences.t:
πεντήκοντά τοί εἰσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναῖκες
δμῳαί, τὰς μέν τ’ ἔργα διδάξαμεν ἐργάζεσθαι,
εἴριά τε ξαίνειν καὶ δουλοσύνην ἀνέχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
pentēkonta toi eisin eni megaroisi gynaikes
dmōiai, tas men t’ erga didaxamen ergazesthai,
eiria te xainein kai doulosynēn anechesthai·
sentences.i: I tell you, there are fifty women in the halls, maidservants whom we have taught to do their work, to card wool and to endure slavery;
sentences.n: τοί is the enclitic 'to you' (σοι), the speaker's emphasis. εἰσίν, after πεντήκοντα, is 'there are'. δμῳαί 'maidservants' stands in apposition to γυναῖκες, and τάς is relative 'whom'. διδάξαμεν is the aorist 'we taught', and the Greek does not say who 'we' are beyond the nurse herself and the household. ἔργα ἐργάζεσθαι is 'to work tasks', an internal accusative. εἴρια is 'wool', and ξαίνω is to comb or card it into a state fit for spinning. δουλοσύνην is 'slavery', and ἀνέχεσθαι 'to endure, put up with', in the sense of the infinitive after 'taught'.

sentences.t:
τάων δώδεκα πᾶσαι ἀναιδείης ἐπέβησαν,
οὔτ’ ἐμὲ τίουσαι οὔτ’ αὐτὴν Πηνελόπειαν.
sentences.tr:
taōn dōdeka pasai anaideiēs epebēsan,
out’ eme tiousai out’ autēn Pēnelopeian.
sentences.l:
Of these, twelve in all have set foot on shamelessness,
neither honouring me nor Penelope herself.
sentences.i: Of these, twelve in all have gone the way of shamelessness, honouring neither me nor Penelope herself.
sentences.n: τάων is the uncontracted genitive plural of the pronoun (Attic τούτων), partitive: 'of these'. ἐπέβησαν is an aorist of ἐπιβαίνω 'step upon', and takes the genitive ἀναιδείης: 'they set foot on shamelessness', that is entered on a course of it. ἀναιδείη is built on ἀναιδής 'shameless'. τίουσαι is the present participle of τίω 'honour', in the nominative feminine plural, agreeing with the unexpressed 'they'.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δὲ νέον μὲν ἀέξετο, οὐδέ ἑ μήτηρ
σημαίνειν εἴασκεν ἐπὶ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos de neon men aexeto, oude he mētēr
sēmainein eiasken epi dmōiēisi gynaixin.
sentences.l:
And Telemachus had only just been growing up, and his mother
would never let him give orders over the maidservant women.
sentences.i: But Telemachus had only just begun to grow up, and his mother never let him give orders to the maidservants.
sentences.n: νέον is the adverb 'newly, lately'. ἀέξετο is the imperfect middle of ἀέξω 'make grow', which in the middle is 'grow'. ἑ is the pronoun 'him'; οὐδέ ἑ is 'nor ... him'. εἴασκεν is an iterative imperfect of ἐάω 'allow', meaning that she never did, again and again. σημαίνειν is 'to give signals, give orders'. ἐπὶ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν is 'over the maidservant women', with δμῳῇσι the dative plural of δμῳή.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ἐγὼν ἀναβᾶσ’ ὑπερώϊα σιγαλόεντα
εἴπω σῇ ἀλόχῳ, τῇ τις θεὸς ὕπνον ἐπῶρσε.
sentences.tr:
all’ ag’ egōn anabas’ hyperōïa sigaloenta
eipō sēi alochōi, tēi tis theos hypnon epōrse.
sentences.l:
But come, I, having gone up to the upper rooms, glossy,
will tell your wife, upon whom some god has stirred up sleep.”
sentences.i: But come, let me go up to the glossy upper rooms and tell your wife, upon whom some god has stirred up sleep.”
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ is 'but come'. ἀναβᾶσ’ is the aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω, 'having gone up', with the final -α elided. ὑπερώϊα are the upper rooms, with σιγαλόεντα 'glossy' as their epithet. εἴπω is an aorist subjunctive of intention, 'let me tell'. ἄλοχος is 'wife' in the dative σῇ ἀλόχῳ. ἐπῶρσε is an aorist of ἐπόρνυμι, 'rouse upon, send upon', so sleep is something a god has sent against her. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: This is a reply-formula already published, and keeps its English. The speech begins in the next line, so the unit is cut at the end of this one. τήν is the pronoun 'her', ἀπαμειβόμενος the participle 'answering', and πολύμητις 'of many wiles', from μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'.

sentences.t: μή πω τήνδ’ ἐπέγειρε·
sentences.tr: mē pō tēnd’ epegeire·
sentences.l: “Not yet rouse this woman;
sentences.i: “Do not wake her yet;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. μή πω with the imperative is 'not yet', and τήνδε 'this woman' points to Penelope upstairs. ἐπέγειρε is the imperative of ἐπεγείρω 'rouse'. The ano teleia falls in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἐνθάδε εἰπὲ γυναιξὶν
ἐλθέμεν, αἵ περ πρόσθεν ἀεικέα μηχανόωντο.
sentences.tr:
sy d’ enthade eipe gynaixin
elthemen, hai per prosthen aeikea mēchanoōnto.
sentences.l:
but you here tell the women
to come, who before devised unseemly things.”
sentences.i: but you, tell the women who earlier devised unseemly things to come here.”
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ ἐνθάδε εἰπὲ γυναιξὶν ἐλθέμεν is 'but you tell the women to come here', the verb εἰπέ followed by the infinitive ἐλθέμεν (Attic ἐλθεῖν). αἵ περ is 'the very ones who'. ἀεικέα, the same word as in 'unseemly doom', is here the neuter plural 'unseemly things'. μηχανόωντο is the imperfect of μηχανάομαι 'devise, contrive', in an uncontracted form. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, γρηῢς δὲ διὲκ μεγάροιο βεβήκει
ἀγγελέουσα γυναιξὶ καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, grēÿs de diek megaroio bebēkei
angeleousa gynaixi kai otryneousa neesthai.
sentences.l:
So then she spoke, and the old woman out through the hall had gone,
to bring word to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and the old woman went out through the hall to carry the message to the women and to urge them to come.
sentences.n: This is a pair of lines already published, and keeps its English. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, without the augment (Attic ἐβεβήκει): 'had gone'. διέκ is διά 'through' with ἐκ 'out', 'out through'. ἀγγελέουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles of purpose in the uncontracted form: 'to bring word', 'to urge'. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι 'go, come'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ Τηλέμαχον καὶ βουκόλον ἠδὲ συβώτην
εἰς ἓ καλεσσάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autar ho Tēlemachon kai boukolon ēde sybōtēn
eis he kalessamenos epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
But he, Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
to himself having called, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: But he called Telemachus, the cowherd and the swineherd to himself and spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', Odysseus. βουκόλος is 'cowherd' and συβώτης 'swineherd'. ἓ is the accusative of the reflexive pronoun, 'himself', and εἰς ἕ is 'to himself'. καλεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of καλέω 'call', with doubled σ. The second line is the formula 'winged words he spoke'.

sentences.t: ἄρχετε νῦν νέκυας φορέειν καὶ ἄνωχθε γυναῖκας·
sentences.tr: archete nyn nekyas phoreein kai anōchthe gynaikas·
sentences.l: “Begin now to carry the corpses, and bid the women;
sentences.i: “Begin now to carry the corpses, and bid the women do so as well;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to the three men. ἄρχετε is the plural imperative 'begin', with the infinitive φορέειν (the uncontracted form of φορεῖν) 'to carry'. ἄνωχθε is the imperative of ἄνωγα 'command, bid'. γυναῖκας is the object of ἄνωχθε; what he bids them is left to be understood from φορέειν, 'to carry', as the women are seen doing at 448, and the infinitive καθαίρειν two lines on completes the order.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα θρόνους περικαλλέας ἠδὲ τραπέζας
ὕδατι καὶ σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι καθαίρειν.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita thronous perikalleas ēde trapezas
hydati kai spongoisi polytrētoisi kathairein.
sentences.l:
but then the very fair chairs and the tables
with water and with sponges full-of-holes to clean.
sentences.i: and after that to clean the very fair chairs and the tables with water and with many-holed sponges.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ἔπειτα is 'but then, next'. The infinitive καθαίρειν 'to clean' belongs to the same order as φορέειν: the women are to clean what the dead men have fouled. περικαλλέας is 'very fair', the fixed rendering of περικαλλής, and θρόνους is 'chairs' (not 'thrones'). σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι, 'sponges full-of-holes' (from πολύς and τρητός 'bored'), is a phrase that has been published before, with 'many-holed sponges' in the plain English. ὕδατι is the dative of ὕδωρ, 'with water'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ πάντα δόμον κατακοσμήσησθε,
δμῳὰς ἐξαγαγόντες ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο,
μεσσηγύς τε θόλου καὶ ἀμύμονος ἕρκεος αὐλῆς,
sentences.tr:
autar epēn dē panta domon katakosmēsēsthe,
dmōias exagagontes eÿstatheos megaroio,
messēgys te tholou kai amymonos herkeos aulēs,
sentences.l:
And when indeed the whole house you have set in order,
and the maidservants having led out of the well-standing hall,
between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
sentences.i: And when you have set the whole house in order and led the maidservants out of the sturdy hall, to the space between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπήν δή is 'and when once'; ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν, and the verb κατακοσμήσησθε is an aorist subjunctive. ἐξαγαγόντες is an aorist participle 'having led out', nominative plural, so the three men are addressed. ἐϋσταθέος is 'well-standing' in the literal English and 'sturdy' in the plain English. θόλος is a round building, a tholos: the Greek does not say what it was used for, and the English names its shape. ἕρκος is a fence or enclosing wall, and ἀμύμων 'blameless' is an epithet whose meaning is not known. Here 'blameless' is kept every time, as the epithet of the fence. αὐλῆς is 'of the courtyard'. The sentence has no main verb yet; it runs on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
θεινέμεναι ξίφεσιν τανυήκεσιν, εἰς ὅ κε πασέων
ψυχὰς ἐξαφέλησθε καὶ ἐκλελάθωντ’ Ἀφροδίτης,
τὴν ἄρ’ ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσιν ἔχον μίσγοντό τε λάθρη.
sentences.tr:
theinemenai xiphesin tanyēkesin, eis ho ke paseōn
psychas exaphelēsthe kai eklelathōnt’ Aphroditēs,
tēn ar’ hypo mnēstērsin echon misgonto te lathrē.
sentences.l:
strike them with long-edged swords, until of all of them
you have taken out the lives, and they have forgotten Aphrodite,
which they were keeping beneath the suitors, and mingled in secret.”
sentences.i: strike them with long-edged swords until you have taken the lives out of all of them and they have forgotten Aphrodite, which they kept beneath the suitors, mingling with them in secret.”
sentences.n: The main verb is here: θεινέμεναι is an infinitive used as an imperative (θείνω 'strike'), in the epic ending -μεναι. τανυήκεσιν, 'long-edged', is built on τανύς 'stretched, long' and a second part that is usually taken as ἀκή 'point, edge'; the formation is not certain, and the English keeps to 'edged'. εἰς ὅ κε with the aorist subjunctive is 'until'. ἐξαφέλησθε is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἐξαφαιρέω 'take out', and πασέων is the uncontracted genitive plural of πᾶς. ψυχάς is 'lives'. ἐκλελάθωντ’ is a reduplicated aorist subjunctive of ἐκλανθάνομαι 'forget', taking the genitive. Ἀφροδίτης stands for love-making, the goddess's domain. τήν refers back to it, and ἔχον ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσιν is 'kept under the suitors', that is while under their sway. μίσγοντο is 'mingled (with them)', λάθρη 'secretly'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἱ δὲ γυναῖκες ἀολλέες ἦλθον ἅπασαι,
αἴν’ ὀλοφυρόμεναι, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσαι.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hai de gynaikes aollees ēlthon hapasai,
ain’ olophyromenai, thaleron kata dakry cheousai.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and the women came all together, every one,
fearsomely wailing, an abundant tear shedding down.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the women came all together, every one, wailing bitterly and shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is 'so he spoke', with the table's English. ἀολλέες is 'all together, in a crowd', and ἅπασαι 'every one'. αἴν’ is αἰνά, neuter plural of αἰνός used as an adverb, 'fearsomely, terribly'; the plain English chooses 'bitterly'. ὀλοφυρόμεναι is the present participle of ὀλοφύρομαι 'wail, lament'. θαλερὸν δάκρυ is 'an abundant tear', where θαλερός is 'abundant'; κατά is with χέουσαι (a participle of χέω 'pour'), 'shedding down'.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν οὖν νέκυας φόρεον κατατεθνηῶτας,
κὰδ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ τίθεσαν εὐερκέος αὐλῆς,
ἀλλήλοισιν ἐρείδουσαι·
sentences.tr:
prōta men oun nekyas phoreon katatethnēōtas,
kad d’ ar’ hyp’ aithousēi tithesan euerkeos aulēs,
allēloisin ereidousai·
sentences.i: First they carried out the corpses, the men who had died, and set them down beneath the portico of the well-fenced courtyard, propping them against one another;
sentences.n: The women are the subject, and the first thing they do is what Odysseus ordered. φόρεον is the imperfect of φορέω 'carry', unaugmented, and κατατεθνηῶτας the perfect participle of καταθνῄσκω 'die', 'those who had died'. κὰδ δ’ ... τίθεσαν is tmesis: κὰδ is κατά with its last letter assimilated to δ, and the verb is καταθέσαν 'set down'; τίθεσαν is an unaugmented imperfect. ὑπ’ αἰθούσῃ is 'beneath the portico'. εὐερκής is from εὖ 'well' and ἕρκος 'fence', 'well-fenced', and agrees with αὐλῆς. ἐρείδουσαι is the present participle of ἐρείδω 'prop, lean, press', here 'propping the bodies one against another'. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σήμαινε δ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
αὐτὸς ἐπισπέρχων·
sentences.tr:
sēmaine d’ Odysseus
autos episperchōn·
sentences.l:
and gave the orders Odysseus
himself, pressing them on;
sentences.i: and Odysseus himself gave the orders, urging them on;
sentences.n: σήμαινε is the imperfect of σημαίνω 'give a sign, give orders'; the same verb stands at 427 in σημαίνειν, of what Telemachus's mother never let him do. αὐτός 'himself' stresses that Odysseus supervises in person, and ἐπισπέρχων is the present participle of ἐπισπέρχω 'urge on, hurry'. The unit begins in the middle of line 450 and ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 451.

sentences.t: ταὶ δ’ ἐκφόρεον καὶ ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.tr: tai d’ ekphoreon kai anankēi.
sentences.l: and they carried them out, even under compulsion.
sentences.i: and they carried them out, even under compulsion.
sentences.n: ταί is the pronoun 'they', the women. ἐκφόρεον is the imperfect of ἐκφορέω 'carry out'. καί here is 'even', and ἀνάγκῃ 'under compulsion', as it is rendered where the word is used elsewhere. The sentence begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia at ἐπισπέρχων.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα θρόνους περικαλλέας ἠδὲ τραπέζας
ὕδατι καὶ σπόγγοισι πολυτρήτοισι κάθαιρον.
sentences.tr:
autar epeita thronous perikalleas ēde trapezas
hydati kai spongoisi polytrētoisi kathairon.
sentences.l:
But then the very fair chairs and the tables
with water and with sponges full-of-holes they cleaned.
sentences.i: Then they cleaned the very fair chairs and the tables with water and with many-holed sponges.
sentences.n: The two lines repeat 438–439, with κάθαιρον, an unaugmented imperfect of καθαίρω, in place of the infinitive: what Odysseus ordered is now done. The English of the lines is the same as there.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Τηλέμαχος καὶ βουκόλος ἠδὲ συβώτης
λίστροισιν δάπεδον πύκα ποιητοῖο δόμοιο
ξῦον·
sentences.tr:
autar Tēlemachos kai boukolos ēde sybōtēs
listroisin dapedon pyka poiētoio domoio
xyon·
sentences.i: Telemachus, the cowherd and the swineherd scraped the floor of the well-built house with shovels;
sentences.n: λίστροισιν is the dative plural of λίστρον, a tool for scraping or levelling a floor: 'shovel' is the nearest English. The floor is δάπεδον, and ποιητοῖο δόμοιο is 'of the well-made house'; πύκα 'closely, firmly' goes with ποιητοῖο, and the English keeps 'close-built' in the literal line and 'well-built' in the free line, as in the other lines with the same words. ξῦον is the unaugmented imperfect of ξύω 'scrape'. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t: ταὶ δ’ ἐφόρεον δμῳαί, τίθεσαν δὲ θύραζε.
sentences.tr: tai d’ ephoreon dmōiai, tithesan de thyraze.
sentences.l: and the maidservants carried it, and put it out of doors.
sentences.i: and the maidservants carried it away and put it outside.
sentences.n: ταὶ δ’ is 'and they'; δμῳαί is in apposition. The Greek does not say what is carried: the object is whatever the shovels removed, and the English supplies 'it'. ἐφόρεον is the imperfect of φορέω, as at 448, and τίθεσαν is an unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι 'put'. θύραζε is 'to the door, out of doors', with the suffix -ζε.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπειδὴ πᾶν μέγαρον διεκοσμήσαντο,
δμῳὰς δ’ ἐξαγαγόντες ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο,
μεσσηγύς τε θόλου καὶ ἀμύμονος ἕρκεος αὐλῆς,
εἴλεον ἐν στείνει, ὅθεν οὔ πως ἦεν ἀλύξαι.
sentences.tr:
autar epeidē pan megaron diekosmēsanto,
dmōias d’ exagagontes eÿstatheos megaroio,
messēgys te tholou kai amymonos herkeos aulēs,
eileon en steinei, hothen ou pōs ēen alyxai.
sentences.l:
But when the whole hall they had set in order,
and the maidservants having led out of the well-standing hall,
between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard,
they penned them in a narrow place, from where in no way was it possible to escape.
sentences.i: But when they had set the whole hall in order and led the maidservants out of the sturdy hall to the space between the round house and the blameless fence of the courtyard, they shut them in a narrow place from which there was no way to escape.
sentences.n: Lines 458–459 repeat 441–442; the English of those lines is kept. διεκοσμήσαντο is an aorist middle of διακοσμέω 'arrange, set in order'. εἴλεον is the imperfect of εἴλω 'shut in, force together'. στεῖνος is a narrow place, here in the dative στείνει. ὅθεν οὔ πως ἦεν ἀλύξαι is 'from which it was not at all possible to escape': ἦεν is the epic ἦν, and ἀλύξαι the aorist infinitive of ἀλύσκω 'escape'. The women are penned in the open yard between the round house and the fence, where there is no way out.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν·
sentences.tr: toisi de Tēlemachos pepnymenos ērch’ agoreuein·
sentences.l: And among them prudent Telemachus began to speak:
sentences.i: And prudent Telemachus was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the pronoun 'to them, among them', the penned women. ἦρχ’ is the imperfect of ἄρχω, 'began', with the infinitive ἀγορεύειν 'to speak'. πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is the epithet of Telemachus, here as elsewhere. The line is a whole-line speech introduction.

sentences.t:
μὴ μὲν δὴ καθαρῷ θανάτῳ ἀπὸ θυμὸν ἑλοίμην
τάων, αἳ δὴ ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ κατ’ ὀνείδεα χεῦαν
μητέρι θ’ ἡμετέρῃ παρά τε μνηστῆρσιν ἴαυον.
sentences.tr:
mē men dē katharōi thanatōi apo thymon heloimēn
taōn, hai dē emēi kephalēi kat’ oneidea cheuan
mēteri th’ hēmeterēi para te mnēstērsin iauon.
sentences.l:
“Not indeed by a clean death may I take the life away
of these women, who upon my head reproaches have poured
and upon our mother, and beside the suitors slept.”
sentences.i: “May I never take the lives of these women by a clean death, women who have poured reproaches on my head and on our mother, and slept beside the suitors.”
sentences.n: Telemachus speaks. μή with the optative ἑλοίμην is a negative wish, 'may I not', and μὲν δή makes it emphatic; the speaker's meaning is that these women will not get an easy death. καθαρῷ θανάτῳ is 'by a clean death', that is a death without a stain of disgrace. ἀπὸ ... ἑλοίμην is tmesis, 'take away', with θυμόν here the life. τάων is the uncontracted genitive plural of the pronoun, 'of those women', and αἳ δή 'who indeed'. χεῦαν is an aorist of χέω 'pour', unaugmented, in the form -αν. ὀνείδεα is 'reproaches'. μητέρι θ’ ἡμετέρῃ is a dative: the reproaches are poured on his mother too. ἴαυον is an imperfect of ἰαύω 'sleep, lie'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, καὶ πεῖσμα νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
κίονος ἐξάψας μεγάλης περίβαλλε θόλοιο,
ὑψόσ’ ἐπεντανύσας, μή τις ποσὶν οὖδας ἵκοιτο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē, kai peisma neos kyanoprōiroio
kionos exapsas megalēs periballe tholoio,
hypsos’ epentanysas, mē tis posin oudas hikoito.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and fastened the cable of a dark-prowed ship to a great pillar and threw it round the round house, stretching it high up, so that none of them could touch the ground with her feet.
sentences.n: πεῖσμα is a ship's mooring-cable; the compound κυανόπρῳρος 'dark-prowed' is the standing epithet of ships. ἐξάψας is the aorist participle of ἐξάπτω 'fasten from, tie to', and the pillar is in the genitive: the cable is tied off from the pillar. περίβαλλε is the imperfect of περιβάλλω 'throw round', with the genitive θόλοιο, 'the round house' (a tholos), as above. The pillar is not otherwise described in this part. ὑψόσ’ is ὑψόσε 'high up', ἐπεντανύσας is the aorist participle of ἐπεντανύω 'stretch taut over', and μή τις ... ἵκοιτο is a negative purpose clause in the optative: 'so that none might reach the ground'. οὖδας is 'ground, floor'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἢ κίχλαι τανυσίπτεροι ἠὲ πέλειαι
ἕρκει ἐνιπλήξωσι, τό θ’ ἑστήκῃ ἐνὶ θάμνῳ,
αὖλιν ἐσιέμεναι, στυγερὸς δ’ ὑπεδέξατο κοῖτος,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an ē kichlai tanysipteroi ēe peleiai
herkei eniplēxōsi, to th’ hestēkēi eni thamnōi,
aulin esiemenai, stygeros d’ hypedexato koitos,
sentences.l:
And as when thrushes, long-winged, or doves
run into a net that stands in a thicket,
to enter their roost, and a hateful bed received them,
sentences.i: As when long-winged thrushes or doves run into a net set up in a thicket as they go in to their roost, and a hateful resting-place receives them,
sentences.n: The simile compares the women's end to the trapping of birds. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν is 'as when', with the subjunctive ἐνιπλήξωσι, 'strike into'. κίχλαι are thrushes, and πέλειαι doves or pigeons. τανυσίπτερος is 'long-winged', from τανύς 'long' and πτερόν 'wing'. ἕρκος is normally a fence or enclosure; here it is a net or snare set up in a bush (θάμνος), and the English says 'net'. ἑστήκῃ is the perfect subjunctive of ἵστημι, 'stands'. αὖλιν is the place where one spends the night, a roost, and ἐσιέμεναι (accented as an infinitive) is the epic infinitive of εἴσειμι 'go in', of purpose: 'to enter'. στυγερός is 'hateful'. κοῖτος is a lying-down place, 'bed'; the roost they were going to enter is replaced by a bed that is a trap.

sentences.t:
ὣς αἵ γ’ ἑξείης κεφαλὰς ἔχον, ἀμφὶ δὲ πάσαις
δειρῇσι βρόχοι ἦσαν, ὅπως οἴκτιστα θάνοιεν.
sentences.tr:
hōs hai g’ hexeiēs kephalas echon, amphi de pasais
deirēisi brochoi ēsan, hopōs oiktista thanoien.
sentences.l:
so they in a row held their heads, and around all
their necks nooses were, so that most pitiably they might die.
sentences.i: so the women held their heads in a row, and around the necks of all of them were nooses, so that they might die in the most pitiable way.
sentences.n: The simile is applied: ὣς αἵ γε 'so they' are the maidservants. ἑξείης is 'in a row, one after another'. ἀμφὶ δὲ πάσαις δειρῇσι is 'around all their necks', with dative plurals in -αις and -ῃσι. βρόχοι ἦσαν is 'there were nooses'. ὅπως with the optative θάνοιεν is 'so that they might die', and οἴκτιστα is the superlative of the adverb from οἶκτος 'pity, lament', 'most pitiable'.

sentences.t: ἤσπαιρον δὲ πόδεσσι μίνυνθά περ οὔ τι μάλα δήν.
sentences.tr: ēspairon de podessi minyntha per ou ti mala dēn.
sentences.l: And they quivered with their feet for a little while, not very long at all.
sentences.i: And they struggled with their feet for a little while, though not for long at all.
sentences.n: ἤσπαιρον is the imperfect of ἀσπαίρω, 'gasp, flutter, struggle convulsively', of a creature that is dying. μίνυνθά περ is 'only for a little while', and οὔ τι μάλα δήν 'not at all very long'. With this line the death of the women is over.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ Μελάνθιον ἦγον ἀνὰ πρόθυρόν τε καὶ αὐλήν·
sentences.tr: ek de Melanthion ēgon ana prothyron te kai aulēn·
sentences.l: And Melanthius they led out through the forecourt and the courtyard;
sentences.i: They led Melanthius out through the forecourt and the courtyard;
sentences.n: The subject 'they' is Telemachus and the two herdsmen. ἐκ ... ἦγον is tmesis, 'led out' (ἐξῆγον), with ἦγον the imperfect. πρόθυρον is the forecourt, the space in front of the hall's door, and αὐλή the courtyard.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ μὲν ῥῖνάς τε καὶ οὔατα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
τάμνον, μήδεά τ’ ἐξέρυσαν, κυσὶν ὠμὰ δάσασθαι,
χεῖράς τ’ ἠδὲ πόδας κόπτον κεκοτηότι θυμῷ.
sentences.tr:
tou d’ apo men rhinas te kai ouata nēleï chalkōi
tamnon, mēdea t’ exerysan, kysin ōma dasasthai,
cheiras t’ ēde podas kopton kekotēoti thymōi.
sentences.l:
From him they cut off both nostrils and ears with pitiless bronze,
and tore out the genitals, raw, for the dogs to divide,
and hands and feet they chopped off with a grudge-bearing heart.
sentences.i: They cut off his nostrils and ears with pitiless bronze, and tore out his genitals, raw, for the dogs to rend among themselves, and chopped off his hands and feet with hearts full of resentment.
sentences.n: Murray prints only commas after τάμνον and ἐξέρυσαν, and the sentence runs to the end of line 477. τοῦ ... ἀπὸ ... τάμνον is tmesis, 'cut off from him'. ῥῖνας are the nostrils. νηλέϊ is 'pitiless', from νηλεής, with χαλκῷ 'bronze' meaning a bronze blade. μήδεα here are the genitals, not the 'counsels' of other lines. δάσασθαι is an aorist infinitive of δατέομαι 'divide, share out', here of purpose. κόπτον is the imperfect of κόπτω 'strike, chop off'. κεκοτηότι θυμῷ is 'with a grudge-bearing heart', from the perfect of κοτέω 'bear a grudge'. The Greek states the mutilation plainly, and the English does the same.

sentences.t:
οἱ μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀπονιψάμενοι χεῖράς τε πόδας τε
εἰς Ὀδυσῆα δόμονδε κίον, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον·
sentences.tr:
hoi men epeit’ aponipsamenoi cheiras te podas te
eis Odysēa domonde kion, tetelesto de ergon·
sentences.l:
They then, having washed off their hands and feet,
went to Odysseus into the house, and the deed was done;
sentences.i: Then they washed their hands and feet and went into the house to Odysseus, and the deed was done;
sentences.n: οἱ μέν is 'they, for their part', the men, set against Odysseus's own action in the next unit. ἀπονιψάμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀπονίζω 'wash off', with the middle meaning they wash their own hands and feet. δόμονδε has the suffix -δε 'to', 'into the house', and κίον is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω 'go'. τετέλεστο is the pluperfect passive of τελέω 'accomplish', and ἔργον 'deed'.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γε προσέειπε φίλην τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν·
sentences.tr: autar ho ge proseeipe philēn trophon Eurykleian·
sentences.l: but he addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: and he spoke to his dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γε is 'but he', Odysseus. The standing description φίλη τροφός 'the dear nurse' is here in the accusative, φίλην τροφὸν Εὐρύκλειαν, the object of προσέειπε 'addressed'. The ano teleia introduces the speech.

sentences.t:
οἶσε θέειον, γρηΰ, κακῶν ἄκος, οἶσε δέ μοι πῦρ,
ὄφρα θεειώσω μέγαρον·
sentences.tr:
oise theeion, grēÿ, kakōn akos, oise de moi pyr,
ophra theeiōsō megaron·
sentences.l:
“Bring sulphur, old woman, a cure for evils, and bring me fire,
so that I may fumigate the hall;
sentences.i: “Bring sulphur, old woman, a cure for ills, and bring me fire, so that I may fumigate the hall;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks again. οἶσε is the aorist imperative of φέρω 'bring', repeated for emphasis. θέειον is sulphur, burned to purify a place. γρηΰ is a vocative 'old woman', a variant spelling of γρηῦ. κακῶν ἄκος is 'a remedy for evils': ἄκος is 'cure, remedy' and κακῶν is the genitive. θεειώσω is an aorist subjunctive of θεειόω, 'treat with sulphur, fumigate', and ὄφρα makes it a purpose clause. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ Πηνελόπειαν
ἐλθεῖν ἐνθάδ’ ἄνωχθι σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί·
sentences.tr:
sy de Pēnelopeian
elthein enthad’ anōchthi syn amphipoloisi gynaixi·
sentences.l:
and you Penelope
bid come here with her attendant women;
sentences.i: and you, tell Penelope to come here with her attendant women;
sentences.n: σὺ δέ is 'and you'. Πηνελόπειαν is the object of ἄνωχθι, the imperative of ἄνωγα 'bid', and ἐλθεῖν is its infinitive, 'to come'. ἐνθάδ’ is ἐνθάδε 'here'. ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξί is 'attendant women', in the dative plural. The sentence begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia at μέγαρον.

sentences.t: πάσας δ’ ὄτρυνον δμῳὰς κατὰ δῶμα νέεσθαι.
sentences.tr: pasas d’ otrynon dmōias kata dōma neesthai.
sentences.l: and urge all the maidservants to come throughout the house.”
sentences.i: and urge all the maidservants to come, through the house.”
sentences.n: ὄτρυνον is the aorist imperative of ὀτρύνω 'urge', and the object is πάσας δμῳάς 'all the maidservants', in the accusative plural δμῳάς. κατὰ δῶμα is 'through the house'. νέεσθαι is the infinitive 'to come', as at 434. This ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then his dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is a whole line already published, and keeps its English. The same line stood at 419 before her first speech.

sentences.t: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε, τέκνον ἐμόν, κατὰ μοῖραν ἔειπες.
sentences.tr: nai dē tauta ge, teknon emon, kata moiran eeipes.
sentences.l: “Yes indeed, these things at least, my child, according to what is fitting you have said.
sentences.i: “Yes indeed, my child, you have spoken these things as is fitting.
sentences.n: Eurycleia answers. ναὶ δή is 'yes indeed', and ταῦτά γε 'these things at least'. κατὰ μοῖραν is the formula 'as is fitting' (the word is μοῖρα 'portion, due', so 'what is due'). ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον with the augment kept (ἔ-ϝειπες), 'you said'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε τοι χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἐνείκω,
μηδ’ οὕτω ῥάκεσιν πεπυκασμένος εὐρέας ὤμους
ἕσταθ’ ἐνὶ μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
all’ age toi chlainan te chitōna te heimat’ eneikō,
mēd’ houtō rhakesin pepykasmenos eureas ōmous
hestath’ eni megaroisi·
sentences.i: But come, let me bring you a cloak and a tunic, garments, and do not stand in the halls like this, your broad shoulders wrapped in rags;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and ἐνείκω, an aorist subjunctive of φέρω, 'let me bring'; τοι is 'to you'. χλαῖναν 'cloak' and χιτῶνα 'tunic' are the two garments, and εἵματα is a general word for 'garments' in apposition. μηδ’ ... ἕσταθ’ is a negative command, with ἕσταθ’ the imperative of ἕστηκα 'stand'. πεπυκασμένος is the perfect participle of πυκάζω 'cover closely', and εὐρέας ὤμους is an accusative of respect, 'as to the broad shoulders'. ῥάκεσιν 'rags' is the dative plural of ῥάκος. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 489.

sentences.t: νεμεσσητὸν δέ κεν εἴη.
sentences.tr: nemessēton de ken eiē.
sentences.l: it would be a thing to resent.”
sentences.i: that would be a thing to resent.”
sentences.n: The unit begins after the ano teleia in the middle of line 489. νεμεσσητόν is 'a thing to resent', from νεμεσσάω 'feel resentment'; κεν εἴη is the optative 'it would be'. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: This is a whole line already published, and keeps its English. It is the same reply-formula as at 430.

sentences.t: πῦρ νῦν μοι πρώτιστον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γενέσθω.
sentences.tr: pyr nyn moi prōtiston eni megaroisi genesthō.
sentences.l: “Fire now for me first of all in the halls let there be.”
sentences.i: “First of all, let there be a fire for me in the halls now.”
sentences.n: Odysseus answers. πῦρ is placed first and is the whole point of the reply: before clothes, fire. γενέσθω is the aorist imperative third singular of γίγνομαι, 'let there be'. πρώτιστον is the adverb 'first of all', a superlative of πρῶτος, and μοι 'for me'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια,
ἤνεικεν δ’ ἄρα πῦρ καὶ θήϊον·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, oud’ apithēse philē trophos Eurykleia,
ēneiken d’ ara pyr kai thēïon·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and did not disobey, the dear nurse Eurycleia,
and she brought fire and sulphur;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his dear nurse Eurycleia did not disobey; she brought fire and sulphur;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he spoke', with the table's English. ἀπίθησε is an aorist of ἀπιθέω 'disobey'; οὐδ’ ἀπίθησε is the usual way of saying 'and she obeyed'. ἤνεικεν is the aorist of φέρω in the form that goes with ἐνείκω above. θήϊον is another form of θέειον, 'sulphur'. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
εὖ διεθείωσεν μέγαρον καὶ δῶμα καὶ αὐλήν.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
eu dietheiōsen megaron kai dōma kai aulēn.
sentences.l:
and Odysseus
thoroughly fumigated the hall and the house and the courtyard.
sentences.i: and Odysseus fumigated the hall, the house and the courtyard thoroughly.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ here means 'and' or 'but' with a change of subject. διεθείωσεν is an aorist of διαθειόω 'fumigate all through', the same verb as θεειώσω in Odysseus's order, with the prefix διά. εὖ is 'well, thoroughly'. μέγαρον is the hall, δῶμα the house as a whole, and αὐλή the courtyard.

sentences.t:
γρηῢς δ’ αὖτ’ ἀπέβη διὰ δώματα κάλ’ Ὀδυσῆος
ἀγγελέουσα γυναιξὶ καὶ ὀτρυνέουσα νέεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
grēÿs d’ aut’ apebē dia dōmata kal’ Odysēos
angeleousa gynaixi kai otryneousa neesthai·
sentences.l:
And the old woman again went away through the fair house of Odysseus
to bring word to the women and to urge them to come;
sentences.i: And the old woman went off again through the fair house of Odysseus, to carry the message to the women and to urge them to come;
sentences.n: The second line is a line already published, and keeps its English. γρηῢς is 'old woman', the nurse. αὖτ’ is αὖτε 'again'. ἀπέβη is the aorist of ἀποβαίνω 'go away'. δώματα is a plural that stands for one house, as μέγαρα does, and κάλ’ is καλά 'fair' with the final vowel elided. Ὀδυσῆος is the genitive of Ὀδυσεύς in the form with a single σ. ἀγγελέουσα and ὀτρυνέουσα are future participles of purpose. The ano teleia at the end of the line is the printed mark.

sentences.t: αἱ δ’ ἴσαν ἐκ μεγάροιο δάος μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαι.
sentences.tr: hai d’ isan ek megaroio daos meta chersin echousai.
sentences.l: And they went out of the hall, torches in their hands holding;
sentences.i: And they went out of the hall, holding torches in their hands;
sentences.n: The women are the maidservants who were not hanged, summoned by the nurse. The line is a line already published, and its English is kept. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go', and δάος is a torch.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἄρ’ ἀμφεχέοντο καὶ ἠσπάζοντ’ Ὀδυσῆα,
καὶ κύνεον ἀγαπαζόμεναι κεφαλήν τε καὶ ὤμους
χεῖράς τ’ αἰνύμεναι·
sentences.tr:
hai men ar’ amphecheonto kai ēspazont’ Odysēa,
kai kyneon agapazomenai kephalēn te kai ōmous
cheiras t’ ainymenai·
sentences.i: And they threw themselves round Odysseus and greeted him, and kissed his head and shoulders, welcoming him gladly, and took hold of his hands;
sentences.n: ἀμφεχέοντο is the imperfect middle of ἀμφιχέω, 'pour round', with the sense 'they flung themselves about him'. ἠσπάζοντο is 'greeted warmly'. κύνεον is the unaugmented imperfect of κυνέω 'kiss', and ἀγαπαζόμεναι is 'gladly welcoming', as in a line already published. The second line is that line, and keeps its English. αἰνύμεναι is the present participle of an old verb 'take, grasp'. The ano teleia falls in mid-line.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ γλυκὺς ἵμερος ᾕρει
κλαυθμοῦ καὶ στοναχῆς, γίγνωσκε δ’ ἄρα φρεσὶ πάσας.
sentences.tr:
ton de glykys himeros hēirei
klauthmou kai stonachēs, gignōske d’ ara phresi pasas.
sentences.l:
and him sweet longing seized
for weeping and groaning, and he knew in his mind every one of them.
sentences.i: and a sweet longing for tears and groans took hold of him, and in his mind he knew them all.
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him'. ᾕρει is the imperfect of αἱρέω 'seize', with its augment made long. ἵμερος is 'longing, desire', and the genitives κλαυθμοῦ καὶ στοναχῆς say what he longed for: 'for weeping and groaning', so the sentence says that he longed to weep. γίγνωσκε is the imperfect of γιγνώσκω 'know, recognise', and φρεσί is the dative plural of φρήν, 'in his mind'. The unit begins after the ano teleia in the middle of line 500, and ends the part.
